The first African American student to attend Stewart Patridge's university, the **University of Mississippi** (Ole Miss), was **James Meredith**.

Meredith became the first Black student admitted to the University of Mississippi on October 1, 1962. His admission was the result of a major civil rights landmark event that involved a federal court order and protection by hundreds of U.S. Marshals, following violent riots on campus that killed two people. He graduated in 1963 with a degree in political science.

**Stewart Patridge** (born December 6, 1974) is an American former footballquarterback best known as the leader of the University of MississippiRebels from 1995 to 1997.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stewart_Patridge#cite_note-1) He won the 1997 Conerly Trophy as the best college football player in the state.
Patridge, a native of Morgan City, Mississippi, attended Pillow Academy, earning three letters in football, baseball and basketball. While an honor roll student at Pillow Academy, Patridge was named All-Conference his junior and senior years, Area Athlete of the Year and team Most Valuable Player his junior and senior years._[citation needed_]
After graduating from high school in 1993, Patridge attended Mississippi Delta Community College, where, as a freshman, he helped lead the football team to a 12-0 record and a national Junior College Championship.  Patridge played for only one year at Mississippi Delta Community College before transferring to the University of Mississippi in Oxford, Mississippi. He earned his first letter in 1996 by playing in 10 of the 11 games, Patridge became the No. 2 quarterback behind Paul Head, taking over in the final three games of the season; and during the 1996 season, Patridge completed 79 of 154 passes for 876 yards with three touchdowns and four interceptions, completing an individual game high of 17 passes for the win against Georgia.

Patridge received numerous awards while playing at the University of Mississippi including the 1997 Ole Miss Quarterback Club Player of the Year, Offensive Player of the Week, Southeastern Conference Player of the Week and was named as the ESPN National Player of the Week after the LSU game when he completed 27 of 43 passes for 346 yards and two touchdowns as the Rebels upset the No. 8 ranked Tigers, 36-21 in Baton Rouge.
Patridge became the only quarterback in Ole Miss history to pass for over 200 yards in nine games in a single season. Patridge also holds the school record for 200 straight passes without an interception.
Patridge, having only started 14 games, ranks 6th for most passes completed, 7th for pass attempts and 7th for passing yards; and
Patridge led the Rebels to a post-season bowl appearance in the first Motor City Bowl. Patridge was named Most Valuable Player as he completed 29 of 47 passes for 332 yards and three touchdowns.
Patridge finished his career at Ole Miss completing 310 of 510 passes for 3,564 yards and 15 touchdowns, giving him a 60.6 completion percentage, which is the third all-time best in Rebel history and making him 8th in school history for total offense.

## Professional career
[edit]
In 1999, Patridge played for the Mississippi Pride in the Regional Football League, where he was named the all-RFL quarterback.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stewart_Patridge#cite_note-2) Then, after the RFL folded, he went to the New England Sea Wolves, the Florida Bobcats and the Carolina Cobras in the Arena Football League from 2000 through 2003.
Patridge is currently_[when?_] living in Olive Branch, Mississippi.

**House Concurrent Resolution 103
_(As Adopted by House and Senate)_**  
A CONCURRENT RESOLUTION COMMENDING STEWART PATRIDGE FOR AN OUTSTANDING FOOTBALL COLLEGIATE CAREER AND FOR RECEIVING THE 1997 "CONERLY TROPHY" AS MISSISSIPPI'S TOP COLLEGIATE PLAYER.

WHEREAS, Mr. Patridge, a native of Morgan City, Mississippi, attended Pillow Academy High School, earning three letters in football, baseball and basketball; and
WHEREAS, while an honor roll student at Pillow Academy, Mr. Patridge was named All-Conference his junior and senior years, Area Athlete of the Year and team Most Valuable Player his junior and senior years; and
WHEREAS, after graduating from high school in 1993, Mr. Patridge attended Mississippi Delta Community College, where he helped lead the football team to a 12-0 record and a national Junior College Championship; and

WHEREAS, in 1995, Mr. Patridge did not play and was redshirted, retaining two years of eligibility to play for the Ole Miss Rebels; and

WHEREAS, earning his first letter in 1996 by playing in 10 of the 11 games, Mr. Patridge became the No. 2 quarterback behind Paul Head, replacing Mr. Head in the final three games of the season; and
WHEREAS, during the 1996 season, Mr. Patridge completed 79 of 154 passes for 876 yards with three touchdowns and four interceptions, completing an individual game high of 17 passes for the win against Georgia; and
WHEREAS, Mr. Patridge received numerous awards while playing at the University of Mississippi including the 1997 Ole Miss Quarterback Club Player of the Year, Offensive Player of the Week, SEC Player of the Week and was named as the ESPN National Player of the Week after the LSU game when he completed 27 of 43 passes for 346 yards and two touchdowns as the Rebels upset the No. 8 ranked Tigers, 36-21 in Baton Rouge; and
WHEREAS, the only quarterback in Ole Miss history to pass for over 200 yards in nine games in a single season, Mr. Patridge also holds the school record for 200 straight passes without an interception; and
WHEREAS, Mr. Patridge, having only started 14 games, ranks 6th for most passes completed, 7th for pass attempts and 7th for passing yards; and
WHEREAS, leading the Rebels to a post-season bowl appearance in the first Ford Motor City Bowl, Mr. Patridge was named Most Valuable Player as he completed 29 of 47 passes for 332 yards and three touchdowns; and
WHEREAS, Mr. Patridge finished his career at Ole Miss completing 310 of 510 passes for 3,564 yards and 15 touchdowns, giving him a 60.6 completion percentage, which is the third all time best in Rebel history and rating him 8th in school history for total offense; and
WHEREAS, the Legislature of the State of Mississippi finds it most appropriate to pay special tribute to such a remarkable athlete as Mr. Stewart Patridge, who has brought great honor to Mississippi through his winning and cooperative spirit and high degree of sportsmanship:

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED BY THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES OF THE STATE OF MISSISSIPPI, THE SENATE CONCURRING THEREIN, That we commend and congratulate Mr. Stewart Patridge, of Morgan City, Mississippi, for an outstanding football collegiate career, for displaying tireless devotion to his athletic endeavors and for receiving the 1997 "Conerly Trophy" as Mississippi's top collegiate player.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, That copies of this resolution be furnished to Mr. Stewart Patridge and the Capitol Press Corps.

# Stephanie Patridge
Visiting Professor
Philosopher in Residence
Biography
Stephanie Patridge joined the faculty at the College of Law in January 2025. She is a philosopher who works on normative issues in the law, culture, and everyday social interactions.She teaches classes in the UI Center for Human Rights.
Prior to coming to the College, she was Chair of the Department of Philosophy and a Coordinator-Liaison to the Arts and Humanities at Otterbein University, where she is an Emerita Professor of Philosophy.
She is currently writing a manuscript on social status and snobbery, and has research projects on expressive content in the law, Aristotle’s virtue of _eutrapelia_(wit), and games and social normativity.She has published articles on a range of topics, including racist and sexist jokes, social status and snobbery, race and gender in video games, and pornography. She is the co-editor of _Aesthetics: A Reader in Philosophy of the Arts_(2018, Routledge).
Learn more about Patridge and her work via Google Scholar and LinkedIn.

WHEREAS, after graduating from high school in 1993, Mr. Patridge attended Mississippi Delta Community College, where he helped lead the football team to a 12-0 record and a national Junior College Championship; and

**Stewart Patridge** (born December 6, 1974) is an American former footballquarterback best known as the leader of the University of MississippiRebels from 1995 to 1997.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stewart_Patridge#cite_note-1) He won the 1997 Conerly Trophy as the best college football player in the state.
Patridge, a native of Morgan City, Mississippi, attended Pillow Academy, earning three letters in football, baseball and basketball. While an honor roll student at Pillow Academy, Patridge was named All-Conference his junior and senior years, Area Athlete of the Year and team Most Valuable Player his junior and senior years._[citation needed_]
After graduating from high school in 1993, Patridge attended Mississippi Delta Community College, where, as a freshman, he helped lead the football team to a 12-0 record and a national Junior College Championship.  Patridge played for only one year at Mississippi Delta Community College before transferring to the University of Mississippi in Oxford, Mississippi. He earned his first letter in 1996 by playing in 10 of the 11 games, Patridge became the No. 2 quarterback behind Paul Head, taking over in the final three games of the season; and during the 1996 season, Patridge completed 79 of 154 passes for 876 yards with three touchdowns and four interceptions, completing an individual game high of 17 passes for the win against Georgia.

Patridge received numerous awards while playing at the University of Mississippi including the 1997 Ole Miss Quarterback Club Player of the Year, Offensive Player of the Week, Southeastern Conference Player of the Week and was named as the ESPN National Player of the Week after the LSU game when he completed 27 of 43 passes for 346 yards and two touchdowns as the Rebels upset the No. 8 ranked Tigers, 36-21 in Baton Rouge.
Patridge became the only quarterback in Ole Miss history to pass for over 200 yards in nine games in a single season. Patridge also holds the school record for 200 straight passes without an interception.
Patridge, having only started 14 games, ranks 6th for most passes completed, 7th for pass attempts and 7th for passing yards; and
Patridge led the Rebels to a post-season bowl appearance in the first Motor City Bowl. Patridge was named Most Valuable Player as he completed 29 of 47 passes for 332 yards and three touchdowns.
Patridge finished his career at Ole Miss completing 310 of 510 passes for 3,564 yards and 15 touchdowns, giving him a 60.6 completion percentage, which is the third all-time best in Rebel history and making him 8th in school history for total offense.

## Professional career
[edit]
In 1999, Patridge played for the Mississippi Pride in the Regional Football League, where he was named the all-RFL quarterback.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stewart_Patridge#cite_note-2) Then, after the RFL folded, he went to the New England Sea Wolves, the Florida Bobcats and the Carolina Cobras in the Arena Football League from 2000 through 2003.
Patridge is currently_[when?_] living in Olive Branch, Mississippi.

Stephanie Patridge joined the faculty at the College of Law in January 2025. She is a philosopher who works on normative issues in the law, culture, and everyday social interactions.She teaches classes in the UI Center for Human Rights.
Prior to coming to the College, she was Chair of the Department of Philosophy and a Coordinator-Liaison to the Arts and Humanities at Otterbein University, where she is an Emerita Professor of Philosophy.
She is currently writing a manuscript on social status and snobbery, and has research projects on expressive content in the law, Aristotle’s virtue of _eutrapelia_(wit), and games and social normativity.She has published articles on a range of topics, including racist and sexist jokes, social status and snobbery, race and gender in video games, and pornography. She is the co-editor of _Aesthetics: A Reader in Philosophy of the Arts_(2018, Routledge).

## University of Mississippi
### Rioting at the University
On Sunday, September 30, 1962, Governor Barnett called the Attorney General, Robert Kennedy, to try to get him to postpone Meredith's admission to the university.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:1-28) The Attorney General refused.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:2-16) Meredith, accompanied by Mississippi Highway Patrol and 500 federal marshals, moved into his dorm room.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:3-24) Outside the Lyceum building, where Meredith was due to register for classes the next day, a crowd of hostile students formed near the marshals who were protecting the building.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:3-24)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:1-28) At 7:30 p.m., the crowd broke into a riot.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:1-28) The crowd, which numbered 3000, threw bottles and rocks, and the marshals tear-gassed them.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:0-26)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:1-28) More than 300 people were injured, and two people were killed.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:0-26)

## University of Mississippi
### Enrollment
The day after the riots, on October 1, 1962, after federal and state forces took control, Meredith became the first African-American student to enroll at the University of Mississippi.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-29) Meredith's admission is regarded as a pivotal moment in the history of civil rights in the United States.
Many students harassed Meredith during his two semesters on campus,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-30) but others accepted him. According to first-person accounts, students living in Meredith's dorm bounced basketballs on the floor just above his room through all hours of the night. Other students ostracized him: when Meredith walked into the cafeteria for meals, the students eating would turn their backs. If Meredith sat at a table with other students, all of whom were white, the students would immediately get up and go to another table.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-31) He persisted through harassment and extreme isolation to graduate on August 18, 1963, with a degree in political science.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-LMAWCR2010-32)

## Education and activism
James Meredith wounded after being shot on June 7, 1966
Meredith continued his education, focusing on political science, at the University of Ibadan in Nigeria.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-33) He returned to the United States in 1965. He attended law school through a scholarship at Columbia University and earned an LL.B (law degree) in 1968.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-34)
In 1966, Meredith organized and led a solo, personal March Against Fear for 220 miles from Memphis, Tennessee, to Jackson, Mississippi, beginning on June 6, 1966. Inviting only black men to join him, he wanted to highlight continuing racial oppression in the Mississippi Delta, as well as to encourage blacks to register and vote following passage of the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965, which authorized federal oversight and enforcement of rights. Governor [Paul Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_B._Johnson,_Jr. "Paul B. Johnson, Jr.") promised to allow the march and provide State Highway Police protection. Meredith wanted blacks in Mississippi to overcome fear of violence._[citation needed_]
Despite a police presence,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-americanheritage.com-35) on the second day, Meredith was shot and wounded by Aubrey James Norvell, a white unemployed hardware clerk whose motives were never determined, and who pleaded guilty at trial.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-36) Meredith was quickly taken to a hospital.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-38) Leaders of major organizations rallied at the news and vowed to complete the march in Meredith's name. They struggled to reconcile differing goals, but succeeded in attracting more than 10,000 marchers from local towns and across the country by the end.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-39)

## Education and activism
Norvell pleaded guilty to battery and assault with intent to kill and was sentenced to five years in prison.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-40) He was released after 18 months, vowing to "live a normal life".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-41)
Meredith suffered from superficial wounds to his neck, legs, head, and right side.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-americanheritage.com-35) He recovered from his wounds, and rejoined the march before it reached Jackson on June 26, when 15,000 marchers entered the city in what had become the largest civil rights march in state history. During the march, more than 4,000 black Mississippians registered to vote. Continued community organizing was catalyzed by these events, and African Americans began to enter the political system again.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-42)

## Political career
In 1967, while living and studying in New York, Meredith decided to run as a Republican against incumbent [Adam Clayton Powell Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Clayton_Powell_Jr. "Adam Clayton Powell Jr."), a multi-term Democrat, in a special election for the Congressional seat in Harlem. He withdrew from the race and Powell was re-elected.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-Jet-43) Meredith said later of his campaign, "The Republican Party [of New York] made me an offer: full support in every way, everything." He had full access to top New York Republicans.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-44)
After returning to Mississippi in 1972, Meredith entered the Republican primary for the U.S. Senate seat of Democrat James Eastland, who had been the incumbent for 29 years in what had operated as a one-party state. Following provisions of a new state constitution in 1890 that made voter registration extremely difficult, African Americans had been effectively disenfranchised and the Republican Party had been crippled.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-45) Meredith conceded that he had little chance of winning unless Governor George Wallace of Alabama entered the presidential race and split the white vote.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-Jet-43) As it happened, many Republicans in Mississippi were not enthusiastic about the prospect of Meredith as their nominee, and Gil Carmichael, a businessman from Meridian, was recruited to run against him.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-46) Meredith received only 21% of the primary vote against Carmichael.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-47)

## About
James H. Meredith (1933– ; Columbia Law School 1968) American civil rights activist who gained national renown at a key juncture in the Civil Rights Movement in 1962, when he became the first African American student at the University of Mississippi. State officials, initially refusing a U.S. Supreme Court order to integrate the school, blocked Meredith’s entrance, but, following large campus riots that left two people dead, Meredith was admitted to the university under the protection of federal marshals.
Before the University of Mississippi,Meredith served in the U.S. Air Force (1951–60), followed by attending an all-black school, Jackson State College (1960–62). His repeated applications to the University of Mississippi were denied solely on the basis of his race, according to the verdict of his 1961–62 court battle, which was won on appeal with the legal assistance of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). In the fall of 1962, as mob violence seemed imminent, U.S. Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy called in federal protection so that Meredith could register for classes. Meredith’s tenure at Mississippi was brief; he graduated in 1963 and wrote a memoir about the experience, called _Three Years in Mississippi._
Meredith continued to balance education and activism throughout the rest of the decade, attending the University of Ibadan in Nigeria (1964–65) and Columbia University (1966–68). In June 1966, he began a solitary protest march, which he called the March Against Fear, from Memphis, Tennessee, to Jackson, Mississippi, when he was shot by a sniper. The crime mobilized many civil rights leaders to resume the march, which Meredith was able to rejoin after a period of hospitalization.

# James Meredith | Life, Civil Rights & Legacy
## Who was James Meredith?
**James Meredith** is best known for being a civil rights activist and a pioneer in the integration of southern universities. Meredith grew up on a farm sheltered from the terrible racism that existed beyond his small community. However, once he experienced it on a train ride, he decided he had to help the civil rights movement. He became the first Black student to be admitted to the University of Mississippi. Being admitted into the University of Mississippi was no easy feat. Meredith had to experience violence, insults, and many court cases before finally taking a class at the university. His publicized experience at the University of Mississippi made him a civil rights icon. Later in life, Meredith was honored with a statue at the University of Mississippi for his courage during that violent time. Meredith was married twice. He married Mary June Wiggins in 1956 and they had three sons. After Mary's death in 1979, Meredith married Judy Alsobrooks, with whom he had a son and a daughter. James Meredith is still alive today, continuing his mission for equality among Americans.

# James Meredith | Life, Civil Rights & Legacy
## Who was James Meredith?
### Early Life and Education
James Meredith was born in Kosciusko, Mississippi on June 25, 1933. He grew up on his family's large farm with his 12 siblings, away from the strife and civil unrest growing throughout the country. However, Meredith could not be hidden from the harsh realities of America for long. As a young man, his first experience with institutionalized racism occurred when he was riding on a train with his brother from Chicago. The train arrived in Memphis, Tennessee, and Meredith was ordered to give up his seat and move to the back, crowded area designated for other Black train riders. He had to stand in that section for the remainder of the train ride home. It was after this experience that Meredith decided to become an activist and fight for civil rights.
Although living on the farm hid him away from the racism he would experience in the city, Meredith did not enjoy farm life. So, his parents sent him to live with his aunt and uncle in St. Petersburg, Florida to attend public school. He graduated from high school in Florida in 1951. Immediately after graduating, Meredith joined the United States Air Force and served nine years.
After his time in the Air Force ended, Meredith returned home to Mississippi and wanted to achieve higher education. He attended Jackson State College, which was an all-Black college. However, after being inspired by John F. Kennedy's inauguration, Meredith applied for admission to the **University of Mississippi**, also known as Ole Miss, in January 1961. He was determined to become the first Black student at the university and challenge the segregationist, racist system in the south. After many court battles, blockages from Mississippi governor Ross Barnett, and violent mobs at the university opposing his attendance, James Meredith became the first Black student to be admitted and attend Ole Miss on October 1, 1962.

# James Meredith | Life, Civil Rights & Legacy
## Meredith and Civil Rights
Meredith's fight to be admitted to, and attend, the University of Mississippi was a crucial turning point in the pursuit of civil rights for African Americans. After the University of Mississippi rejected his application twice, Meredith became determined to be admitted. He wanted to attack segregation practices in the South, starting with their education policies. The NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People) helped Meredith file a lawsuit against University of Mississippi. Meredith's lawsuit argued that the university's refusal to admit him because of his skin color was against the Supreme Court ruling _Brown v. Board of Education_, which banned the segregation of races in schools. The district and state courts ruled against him but Meredith and his attorneys did not quit. They appealed those rulings and Meredith's lawsuit reached the Supreme Court, which ruled that the university had to allow Meredith to be admitted.
James Meredith helped to propel the civil rights movement forward through the desegregation of southern colleges and universities. He was determined to gain equality and respect for Black Americans. In the pursuit of this mission, he suffered abuse and violence from those who wanted to uphold Jim Crow segregation. While he tried to enroll in classes at the University of Mississippi, he was met with violent mobs, cherry bombs, water balloons, and endless taunts. However, he did not allow that to stop him from becoming the first Black student at the university and being one step closer to helping gain equality for all Americans through attending school there.
James Meredith fought to end segregation in the higher institutions of the American South.
After his traumatic time at the University of Mississippi, Meredith became a lawyer and continued with his activism. This time he became a voting rights activist. He also created his own march that he named the **"March Against Fear."** It would start in Tennessee and end in Mississippi. Shortly into his march, Meredith was shot by a sniper. While he was hospitalized, other notable civil rights activists marched in his place, such as Martin Luther King and Stokely Carmichael. For the rest of his life, Meredith continued his activism and his passion for civil rights. As a local leader in Mississippi, he organized another march, the "Black Man's March to the Library," to help promote the reading and writing of English for everyone. He also created the "Black Man's March for Education to the University of Mississippi."

## University of Mississippi
### Rioting at the University
On Sunday, September 30, 1962, Governor Barnett called the Attorney General, Robert Kennedy, to try to get him to postpone Meredith's admission to the university.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:1-28) The Attorney General refused.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:2-16) Meredith, accompanied by Mississippi Highway Patrol and 500 federal marshals, moved into his dorm room.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:3-24) Outside the Lyceum building, where Meredith was due to register for classes the next day, a crowd of hostile students formed near the marshals who were protecting the building.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:3-24)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:1-28) At 7:30 p.m., the crowd broke into a riot.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:1-28) The crowd, which numbered 3000, threw bottles and rocks, and the marshals tear-gassed them.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:0-26)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:1-28) More than 300 people were injured, and two people were killed.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-:0-26)

## University of Mississippi
### Enrollment
The day after the riots, on October 1, 1962, after federal and state forces took control, Meredith became the first African-American student to enroll at the University of Mississippi.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-29) Meredith's admission is regarded as a pivotal moment in the history of civil rights in the United States.
Many students harassed Meredith during his two semesters on campus,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-30) but others accepted him. According to first-person accounts, students living in Meredith's dorm bounced basketballs on the floor just above his room through all hours of the night. Other students ostracized him: when Meredith walked into the cafeteria for meals, the students eating would turn their backs. If Meredith sat at a table with other students, all of whom were white, the students would immediately get up and go to another table.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-31) He persisted through harassment and extreme isolation to graduate on August 18, 1963, with a degree in political science.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-LMAWCR2010-32)

## Education and activism
James Meredith wounded after being shot on June 7, 1966
Meredith continued his education, focusing on political science, at the University of Ibadan in Nigeria.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-33) He returned to the United States in 1965. He attended law school through a scholarship at Columbia University and earned an LL.B (law degree) in 1968.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-34)
In 1966, Meredith organized and led a solo, personal March Against Fear for 220 miles from Memphis, Tennessee, to Jackson, Mississippi, beginning on June 6, 1966. Inviting only black men to join him, he wanted to highlight continuing racial oppression in the Mississippi Delta, as well as to encourage blacks to register and vote following passage of the federal Voting Rights Act of 1965, which authorized federal oversight and enforcement of rights. Governor [Paul Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_B._Johnson,_Jr. "Paul B. Johnson, Jr.") promised to allow the march and provide State Highway Police protection. Meredith wanted blacks in Mississippi to overcome fear of violence._[citation needed_]
Despite a police presence,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-americanheritage.com-35) on the second day, Meredith was shot and wounded by Aubrey James Norvell, a white unemployed hardware clerk whose motives were never determined, and who pleaded guilty at trial.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-36) Meredith was quickly taken to a hospital.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-38) Leaders of major organizations rallied at the news and vowed to complete the march in Meredith's name. They struggled to reconcile differing goals, but succeeded in attracting more than 10,000 marchers from local towns and across the country by the end.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-39)

## Education and activism
Norvell pleaded guilty to battery and assault with intent to kill and was sentenced to five years in prison.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-40) He was released after 18 months, vowing to "live a normal life".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-41)
Meredith suffered from superficial wounds to his neck, legs, head, and right side.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-americanheritage.com-35) He recovered from his wounds, and rejoined the march before it reached Jackson on June 26, when 15,000 marchers entered the city in what had become the largest civil rights march in state history. During the march, more than 4,000 black Mississippians registered to vote. Continued community organizing was catalyzed by these events, and African Americans began to enter the political system again.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-42)
texts.13:
## Political career
In 1967, while living and studying in New York, Meredith decided to run as a Republican against incumbent [Adam Clayton Powell Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Clayton_Powell_Jr. "Adam Clayton Powell Jr."), a multi-term Democrat, in a special election for the Congressional seat in Harlem. He withdrew from the race and Powell was re-elected.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-Jet-43) Meredith said later of his campaign, "The Republican Party [of New York] made me an offer: full support in every way, everything." He had full access to top New York Republicans.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-44)
After returning to Mississippi in 1972, Meredith entered the Republican primary for the U.S. Senate seat of Democrat James Eastland, who had been the incumbent for 29 years in what had operated as a one-party state. Following provisions of a new state constitution in 1890 that made voter registration extremely difficult, African Americans had been effectively disenfranchised and the Republican Party had been crippled.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-45) Meredith conceded that he had little chance of winning unless Governor George Wallace of Alabama entered the presidential race and split the white vote.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-Jet-43) As it happened, many Republicans in Mississippi were not enthusiastic about the prospect of Meredith as their nominee, and Gil Carmichael, a businessman from Meridian, was recruited to run against him.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-46) Meredith received only 21% of the primary vote against Carmichael.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-47)

**James Meredith** is best known for being a civil rights activist and a pioneer in the integration of southern universities. Meredith grew up on a farm sheltered from the terrible racism that existed beyond his small community. # James Meredith | Life, Civil Rights & Legacy
## Who was James Meredith?
### Early Life and Education
James Meredith was born in Kosciusko, Mississippi on June 25, 1933. He grew up on his family's large farm with his 12 siblings, away from the strife and civil unrest growing throughout the country. However, Meredith could not be hidden from the harsh realities of America for long. As a young man, his first experience with institutionalized racism occurred when he was riding on a train with his brother from Chicago. The train arrived in Memphis, Tennessee, and Meredith was ordered to give up his seat and move to the back, crowded area designated for other Black train riders. He had to stand in that section for the remainder of the train ride home. It was after this experience that Meredith decided to become an activist and fight for civil rights.
Although living on the farm hid him away from the racism he would experience in the city, Meredith did not enjoy farm life. So, his parents sent him to live with his aunt and uncle in St. Petersburg, Florida to attend public school. He graduated from high school in Florida in 1951. Immediately after graduating, Meredith joined the United States Air Force and served nine years.
After his time in the Air Force ended, Meredith returned home to Mississippi and wanted to achieve higher education. He attended Jackson State College, which was an all-Black college. However, after being inspired by John F. Kennedy's inauguration, Meredith applied for admission to the **University of Mississippi**, also known as Ole Miss, in January 1961. He was determined to become the first Black student at the university and challenge the segregationist, racist system in the south. After many court battles, blockages from Mississippi governor Ross Barnett, and violent mobs at the university opposing his attendance, James Meredith became the first Black student to be admitted and attend Ole Miss on October 1, 1962.

# James Meredith | Life, Civil Rights & Legacy
## Meredith and Civil Rights
Meredith's fight to be admitted to, and attend, the University of Mississippi was a crucial turning point in the pursuit of civil rights for African Americans. After the University of Mississippi rejected his application twice, Meredith became determined to be admitted. He wanted to attack segregation practices in the South, starting with their education policies. The NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People) helped Meredith file a lawsuit against University of Mississippi. Meredith's lawsuit argued that the university's refusal to admit him because of his skin color was against the Supreme Court ruling _Brown v. Board of Education_, which banned the segregation of races in schools. The district and state courts ruled against him but Meredith and his attorneys did not quit. They appealed those rulings and Meredith's lawsuit reached the Supreme Court, which ruled that the university had to allow Meredith to be admitted.
James Meredith helped to propel the civil rights movement forward through the desegregation of southern colleges and universities. He was determined to gain equality and respect for Black Americans. In the pursuit of this mission, he suffered abuse and violence from those who wanted to uphold Jim Crow segregation. While he tried to enroll in classes at the University of Mississippi, he was met with violent mobs, cherry bombs, water balloons, and endless taunts. However, he did not allow that to stop him from becoming the first Black student at the university and being one step closer to helping gain equality for all Americans through attending school there.
James Meredith fought to end segregation in the higher institutions of the American South.
After his traumatic time at the University of Mississippi, Meredith became a lawyer and continued with his activism. This time he became a voting rights activist. He also created his own march that he named the **"March Against Fear."** It would start in Tennessee and end in Mississippi. Shortly into his march, Meredith was shot by a sniper. While he was hospitalized, other notable civil rights activists marched in his place, such as Martin Luther King and Stokely Carmichael. For the rest of his life, Meredith continued his activism and his passion for civil rights. As a local leader in Mississippi, he organized another march, the "Black Man's March to the Library," to help promote the reading and writing of English for everyone. He also created the "Black Man's March for Education to the University of Mississippi."

## About
James H. Meredith (1933– ; Columbia Law School 1968) American civil rights activist who gained national renown at a key juncture in the Civil Rights Movement in 1962, when he became the first African American student at the University of Mississippi. State officials, initially refusing a U.S. Supreme Court order to integrate the school, blocked Meredith’s entrance, but, following large campus riots that left two people dead, Meredith was admitted to the university under the protection of federal marshals.
Before the University of Mississippi,Meredith served in the U.S. Air Force (1951–60), followed by attending an all-black school, Jackson State College (1960–62). His repeated applications to the University of Mississippi were denied solely on the basis of his race, according to the verdict of his 1961–62 court battle, which was won on appeal with the legal assistance of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). In the fall of 1962, as mob violence seemed imminent, U.S. Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy called in federal protection so that Meredith could register for classes. Meredith’s tenure at Mississippi was brief; he graduated in 1963 and wrote a memoir about the experience, called _Three Years in Mississippi._
Meredith continued to balance education and activism throughout the rest of the decade, attending the University of Ibadan in Nigeria (1964–65) and Columbia University (1966–68). In June 1966, he began a solitary protest march, which he called the March Against Fear, from Memphis, Tennessee, to Jackson, Mississippi, when he was shot by a sniper. The crime mobilized many civil rights leaders to resume the march, which Meredith was able to rejoin after a period of hospitalization.

The day after the riots, on October 1, 1962, after federal and state forces took control, Meredith became the first African-American student to enroll at the University of Mississippi.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-29) Meredith's admission is regarded as a pivotal moment in the history of civil rights in the United States.

Norvell pleaded guilty to battery and assault with intent to kill and was sentenced to five years in prison.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-40) He was released after 18 months, vowing to "live a normal life".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-41)

## Political career
In 1967, while living and studying in New York, Meredith decided to run as a Republican against incumbent [Adam Clayton Powell Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam_Clayton_Powell_Jr. "Adam Clayton Powell Jr."), a multi-term Democrat, in a special election for the Congressional seat in Harlem. Following provisions of a new state constitution in 1890 that made voter registration extremely difficult, African Americans had been effectively disenfranchised and the Republican Party had been crippled.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-45) Meredith conceded that he had little chance of winning unless Governor George Wallace of Alabama entered the presidential race and split the white vote.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-Jet-43) As it happened, many Republicans in Mississippi were not enthusiastic about the prospect of Meredith as their nominee, and Gil Carmichael, a businessman from Meridian, was recruited to run against him.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-46) Meredith received only 21% of the primary vote against Carmichael.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Meredith#cite_note-47)

# James Meredith | Life, Civil Rights & Legacy
## Who was James Meredith?
**James Meredith** is best known for being a civil rights activist and a pioneer in the integration of southern universities. Meredith grew up on a farm sheltered from the terrible racism that existed beyond his small community. However, once he experienced it on a train ride, he decided he had to help the civil rights movement. He became the first Black student to be admitted to the University of Mississippi. Being admitted into the University of Mississippi was no easy feat. Meredith had to experience violence, insults, and many court cases before finally taking a class at the university. His publicized experience at the University of Mississippi made him a civil rights icon. Later in life, Meredith was honored with a statue at the University of Mississippi for his courage during that violent time. Meredith was married twice. He married Mary June Wiggins in 1956 and they had three sons. After Mary's death in 1979, Meredith married Judy Alsobrooks, with whom he had a son and a daughter. James Meredith is still alive today, continuing his mission for equality among Americans.

## Who was James Meredith?
### Early Life and Education
James Meredith was born in Kosciusko, Mississippi on June 25, 1933. He grew up on his family's large farm with his 12 siblings, away from the strife and civil unrest growing throughout the country. However, Meredith could not be hidden from the harsh realities of America for long. As a young man, his first experience with institutionalized racism occurred when he was riding on a train with his brother from Chicago. The train arrived in Memphis, Tennessee, and Meredith was ordered to give up his seat and move to the back, crowded area designated for other Black train riders. He had to stand in that section for the remainder of the train ride home. It was after this experience that Meredith decided to become an activist and fight for civil rights.
Although living on the farm hid him away from the racism he would experience in the city, Meredith did not enjoy farm life. So, his parents sent him to live with his aunt and uncle in St. Petersburg, Florida to attend public school. He graduated from high school in Florida in 1951. Immediately after graduating, Meredith joined the United States Air Force and served nine years.
After his time in the Air Force ended, Meredith returned home to Mississippi and wanted to achieve higher education. He attended Jackson State College, which was an all-Black college. However, after being inspired by John F. Kennedy's inauguration, Meredith applied for admission to the **University of Mississippi**, also known as Ole Miss, in January 1961. He was determined to become the first Black student at the university and challenge the segregationist, racist system in the south. After many court battles, blockages from Mississippi governor Ross Barnett, and violent mobs at the university opposing his attendance, James Meredith became the first Black student to be admitted and attend Ole Miss on October 1, 1962.

# James Meredith | Life, Civil Rights & Legacy
## Meredith and Civil Rights
Meredith's fight to be admitted to, and attend, the University of Mississippi was a crucial turning point in the pursuit of civil rights for African Americans. After the University of Mississippi rejected his application twice, Meredith became determined to be admitted. He wanted to attack segregation practices in the South, starting with their education policies. The NAACP (National Association for the Advancement of Colored People) helped Meredith file a lawsuit against University of Mississippi. Meredith's lawsuit argued that the university's refusal to admit him because of his skin color was against the Supreme Court ruling _Brown v. Board of Education_, which banned the segregation of races in schools. The district and state courts ruled against him but Meredith and his attorneys did not quit. They appealed those rulings and Meredith's lawsuit reached the Supreme Court, which ruled that the university had to allow Meredith to be admitted.
James Meredith helped to propel the civil rights movement forward through the desegregation of southern colleges and universities. He was determined to gain equality and respect for Black Americans. In the pursuit of this mission, he suffered abuse and violence from those who wanted to uphold Jim Crow segregation. While he tried to enroll in classes at the University of Mississippi, he was met with violent mobs, cherry bombs, water balloons, and endless taunts. However, he did not allow that to stop him from becoming the first Black student at the university and being one step closer to helping gain equality for all Americans through attending school there.
James Meredith fought to end segregation in the higher institutions of the American South.
After his traumatic time at the University of Mississippi, Meredith became a lawyer and continued with his activism. This time he became a voting rights activist. He also created his own march that he named the **"March Against Fear."** It would start in Tennessee and end in Mississippi. Shortly into his march, Meredith was shot by a sniper. While he was hospitalized, other notable civil rights activists marched in his place, such as Martin Luther King and Stokely Carmichael. For the rest of his life, Meredith continued his activism and his passion for civil rights. As a local leader in Mississippi, he organized another march, the "Black Man's March to the Library," to help promote the reading and writing of English for everyone. He also created the "Black Man's March for Education to the University of Mississippi."
